problem: Deployment-time adaptation for VLN (TENT, FSTTA, ATENA, FeedTTA) relies on self-supervised entropy signals or coarse success/failure feedback, which are noisy and cause error self-reinforcement in long-horizon decisions, giving only marginal gains.
motivation: Real-world agents face unseen scenes, visually similar rooms and user-specific language, and drift off the instruction early, with errors compounding. User feedback (success confirmation and goal correction) is intent-aligned, in-situ consistent and interaction-sparse, so it could give reliable supervision if the sparse goal signal is turned into dense path supervision.
key_idea: Use episode-level user feedback (success confirmation or the correct goal viewpoint) and lift it to path-level imitation supervision via A* on the agent's own incrementally built topological graph, with a reloadable memory bank for warm start.
insight: Reliable external supervision beats self-supervision: entropy-based TTA on GR-DUET adds only +0.37 to +0.50 SR, while feedback-driven adaptation adds +9.37 SR (w/o Mem). The ablation shows that more executed instructions (denser graph, coverage 76.6% to 94.1%) and more feedback are complementary, and even 100 feedback samples gives large gains. Filtering to strictly shortest-path samples gives nearly identical results (SR 76.33 / SPL 71.14 vs 70.99), so episode-level lifted paths are not harmful noise.
method: Feedback formalism: at the terminal step the user returns the true goal v* if the agent failed, or confirms the stop; the endpoint v̂ = F(v_T, v*) is used as supervision.

Stage 1 topology and memory: the agent incrementally builds a topological graph G, caches panoramic features/positional encodings C and candidate mappings S (GR-DUET memory M'=(G,C,S)), made persistently reloadable.
Stage 2 trajectory lifting: τ+ = A*(v1→v̂, G) on the built graph, forming (instruction, path) pairs; length-based outlier rejection keeps only paths with 5–7 nodes (removes 5.5%).
Stage 3 adaptation: fine-tune GR-DUET with the imitation loss (DAgger with oracle actions), mixed with source-domain R2R + augmented data for replay to avoid overfitting.
Memory-bank warm start: reload the saved G/C/S when redeploying after an update to avoid cold-start degradation.
Continual adaptation: sequential updates per user (Basic→UserA→UserB, ~500 feedback samples each).
Hybrid adaptation: aggregate feedback from 5 users (500 samples total) into a single update.

setting.backbone: GR-DUET (graph-memory DUET, fine-tuned with user feedback)

results: On GSA-Basic test, feedback adaptation reaches SR 79.04 / SPL 74.40 with memory (76.33 / 70.99 without), versus GR-DUET 66.96 / 61.22 and the best TTA baseline TENT 67.46 / 61.65. Hybrid adaptation on the mixed User split gives +9.91 SR over GR-DUET (61.52→71.43), and continual adaptation improves +1.31 SR over one-step fine-tuning.
limitations: Feedback is simulated using GT goal viewpoints, and evaluation is only in static simulated GSA-R2R residential scenes with no real users or robots.
Adaptation is expensive (~82 h per stage on an RTX 4090, ~246 h for three stages), and the trajectory lifting depends on topology completeness (outliers arise from incomplete graphs).
Comparison against TTA baselines uses different supervision (GT goal feedback), so it is not an equal-information comparison.
